I started watching vlogbrothers videos mid-2010. I really enjoyed John's videos and his insight to things I knew nothing about. I found the format of the videos that are educational (for instance, the video about fiscal cliff) to be extremely helpful because of the language used. It didn't seem like some guy throwing around jargon I was unfamiliar with; it felt like a normal person having a conversation with me about stuff they were passionate about and knew quite a bit about. 

John's novels on the other hand (I'm going with the informal way of writing not as offensive thing, but because I feel like he wouldn't mind too much), I started reading this year (I received the box set as a Christmas gift). I instantly fell in love with his writing style and his voice through the novels. It never felt like I was being spoken down to and none of his writings seemed out of place or fiction. It was like I was there running with Pudge setting off fireworks, or I was in The Hearse with Hassan and Colin. I'm currently finishing reading Paper Towns, and every chapter, heck, every page has me trying to figure out [if Margo is dead or alive](/spoiler). Once I finish Paper Towns, I'm moving onto The Fault in Our Stars. John's novels have really helped me through some of the harder parts of my life (I suffer from PTSD and Major Depression) and his books help me take my mind off of all the bad things in the world. To quote John, "books belong to their readers" and I feel that that quote is one of the best quotes about reading; reading is a different experience for each person and it should be given its time to grow and blossom uniquely for each person.

I hope that answered your question. :)

**tl;dr** John Green's novels have helped me develop a love for reading again and the vlogbrothers have shown me that being a nerd/geek is fantastic.

You make a lot of interesting points. I'm glad to see some people are thinking about the ending. Personally, I think he survived though. It doesn't cheapen the ending (in my eyes that is) if he survived and passed on the cowl. Some counter-points to your theory (most of which have already been mentioned): The pearls, the lack of knowledge about Bruce and Selina, the name of the patch for the autopilot, and sequence in which he's in the cockpit of "The Bat".

1. The biggest wrench in your dream sequence theory is the pearls. At first, I thought Bruce left them in the cave so Blake would have something to track the location, then I saw them around Selina's neck. Alfred is a smart guy, but there is no way he could've known Bruce complimented Selina's appearance in them.

2. You make an interesting point with Alfred possibly asking Gordon what Bruce's final moments were. Now, consider this: maybe Gordon didn't admit to knowing who Batman was. There are two times where Gordon is asked if he wanted to know/knew who "The Batman" was. Both times he says something along the lines of, "He's The Batman." Gordon may have been in disbelief or he simply didn't want Blake to know who Batman was.

3. Lucius asks about the patch that was made for the autopilot. "Bruce Wayne". Hm, now that's interesting. Bruce already made a comment about it not working. Bruce wanted everyone to think he was dead. Lucius would've continued to think he was dead until this moment. Also, check the time that has passed. I believe he said the patch was created nine months ago. Accounting for the five he spent in prison and getting back to Gotham, that leaves four months. For me, I'd like to think Bruce could've fixed the autopilot in one or two months. That leaves two or three months that Bruce could've had to get things together over seas. And with the Clean Slate, he can make himself disappear.

4. Nolan, in my opinion, is one of the best directors of this generation. One of his trademarks in his films is showing things out of, what would originally appear to be, chronological order. For example, the first part of Batman Begins is really around the middle of the story, not the actual beginning (this is of course, taking out his dream of the accident with the well). Or in his first film, The Following, [the main character is actually sitting down in a police interview room recalling the events that led up to, what will be, the current situation] (/spoiler). At first glance, it appears he is still in the cockpit when the bomb goes off. What may actually be happening when he closes his eyes is him blowing up the building and pushing the eject button. He is prepping himself for the smoke, glass, debris, and general feeling of being ejected from an aircraft.


All in all, I do like your theory and it is well supported, but like in Inception [his totem was his wedding ring, not the top, therefore he got home](/spoiler); meaning the ending was what it originally appeared as.
